notes.meaning: King Hezekiah became so sick that he was going to die. Isaiah told him to "put his house in order." That meant making his last wishes known and settling who would rule after him, since he had no son yet. Even great and godly people get sick and die, and being ready for death does not bring it sooner. It only makes it easier to face.

In those days couches ran along the walls of a room. By turning to the wall, Hezekiah turned away from the people around him so he could be alone with God. Some think he may also have turned toward the temple. When trouble comes, prayer is the first place a child of God should go.

Hezekiah was not boasting or trying to earn God's favor. He asked God to remember that he had lived honestly and with a whole heart. "Wholehearted" means sincere, not sinless. He wept hard because he was dying in the prime of life with no heir to the throne. In this way he held on to hope that God had not rejected him.

God answered quickly. Second Kings says it happened before Isaiah had even left the palace courtyard. God did not truly change His mind. His warning had an unspoken condition, and He used it to humble Hezekiah and bring him to pray.

God calls Himself "the God of your father David" to remind Hezekiah of His promise to David's family. God heard the prayer and saw the tears, and He gave fifteen more years. God does not always heal us this way. But He still answers when He gives us strength in our souls, forgives our sins, and holds us as His own whether we live or die.

Along with longer life, God promised to protect Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Assyria. The Assyrians might have come back to take revenge for their defeat. God promised the king peace from them for the rest of his life.

Hezekiah had asked for a sign (see verse 22). That came from weak faith, not unbelief. The "stairway of Ahaz" was probably a set of steps that worked like a sundial, so a shadow showed the time of day. God made the shadow go back ten steps. Some older commentators thought God may have done this by bending the light, but they still saw it as a true miracle. The lesson is plain: God can turn back the hours, so He can lengthen a life.

After he got well, Hezekiah wrote a song. It is found only here, not in Kings or Chronicles. He wrote it down so that he and others would remember both his weakness and God's kindness. Sadly, Scripture says he later failed to stay thankful. Giving thanks is good, but living thankfully is better.
"Sheol" means the grave, the place of the dead. Hezekiah was about 39 years old and expected many more years. He felt his life was being cut off in the middle. He took it as God's judgment on him.

What grieved him most was losing the chance to worship God in the temple here on earth. He still hoped to see God after death, but not "in the land of the living." He would also no longer see his friends or the people he served. A good person wants to live mainly to serve God and walk with Him.

Hezekiah uses two pictures. His life is like a shepherd's tent, quickly pulled down and moved. It is also like cloth on a loom that the weaver rolls up and cuts off when it is finished. Our times are in God's hand, and He decides the length of the cloth. "From day until night" means very quickly.

He tried to stay calm through the night. But the pain crushed him like a lion breaking bones. Each day he thought it would be his last. Henry adds that when we are sick, it matters more how we get safely to the next world than how long we will live in this one.

He was so weak he could not form words. He could only chirp and moan like a bird. Yet God hears even groans that have no words. Though his eyes were worn out, he kept looking up to heaven. "Be my security" is like asking someone to stand bail or pay a debt for you. Henry sees in it a picture of Christ doing for us what we cannot do.

Henry reads this as amazed thanks: God promised to heal him and kept His word. So Hezekiah will walk humbly and carefully all his years, keeping the lesson of his suffering. Calvin reads it instead as Hezekiah still in his grief. On that reading, God has acted, so there is no use arguing, and he expects to walk trembling the rest of his life.

"By such things" means God's promises and His faithful keeping of them. God's word is what truly gives people life, body and spirit. That is why one word from God could bring Hezekiah back from the edge of death.

His bitter suffering turned out for his good. God's love pulled him out of the pit of death. Casting his sins "behind Your back" means God no longer looks at them or holds them against him. Hezekiah valued God's forgiveness even more than his restored life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching separates forgiveness of the guilt of sin from release from all its punishment. Calvin used this verse to argue against that view.

notes.meaning: The dead cannot praise God among people on earth or tell others about Him. Hezekiah was not denying life after death. Faithful souls in heaven do praise God. He meant that death would end his work of honoring God in this world.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars see here the dim, gloomy Old Testament picture of life after death. In their view, this picture was cleared up only later in God's unfolding plan.

notes.meaning: Life is a gift that lets us praise God, and Hezekiah does so "today." Parents are to tell their children about God's faithfulness. Yet Hezekiah's own son Manasseh did not follow God. Parents can give good teaching and example, but they cannot give grace.

The LORD was a ready, present help. So Hezekiah, as leader of his family and people, will lead songs of thanks in the temple for the rest of his life. Special mercies should be thanked for in public worship, where God's people praise Him together.

This verse and the next go back to an earlier point in the story, before the sign. Isaiah told them to put pressed figs on the boil, a known way to soften and draw out a sore. God's promises do not replace using ordinary means like medicine. Instead, they encourage us to use them while trusting God.

Hezekiah had asked for the sign before it was given in verses 7-8. He spoke of going "up to the house of the LORD." That shows what he most wanted his life back for: to worship God and give thanks among His people.
